extracted.intended_audience: program committee chairs, conference and journal editors/associate editors, RMS developers, and members of academic societies concerned with peer review
extracted.subtask_short: automating COI management in peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for detecting, reporting, and managing conflicts of interest (COI) in peer-reviewed venues, with emphasis on automated tools and policy design to supplement/replace manual checking. Targets conference and journal review management workflows, detection algorithms, and reporting/visualization for decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Conflict of Interest (COI)
rubrics_metrics.description: A COI is a set of circumstances that creates a risk that professional judgement or actions regarding a primary interest will be unduly influenced by a secondary interest. Primary interest refers to the principal goals of the profession or activity (e.g., unbiased review); secondary interest includes personal benefits such as financial gain, professional advancement, favors for family, friends, or collaborators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this operational definition as the baseline for determining COI. Note: hiding or falsifying a stated COI is a violation of the ACM Code of Ethics. The definition emphasizes risk of undue influence rather than proven misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized COI types (explicit criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical COI exists if people wrote a paper together in the past x years, are at the same institution currently or in the near past/near future, are close relatives or friends, are advisor and (former) advisee, or worked together closely on a project in the past y years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these categories as the standard checklist of explicit ties that create COI under most venue policies. Implement automated checks for co-authorship and institutional co-affiliation first, and allow policy configuration for year thresholds (x,y).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author self-reporting of COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are typically required to self-report COI with potential program committee (PC) members in current practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-reporting is necessary but insufficient: PC chairs cannot realistically double-check all declarations across many submissions, and manual systems miss unreported COI. Automated validation should complement self-reports rather than replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness: detection of unreported COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems must detect COI that authors did not report; manual checking misses non-negligible numbers of unreported COI (e.g., post-facto checks found violations in ICDE 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by the number of unreported COI detected and by reductions in post-facto discoveries. Integrate automated detection into assignment workflows so undeclared ties are flagged early for PC chair review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust name and affiliation matching
rubrics_metrics.description: COI detection needs to handle free-form names and affiliations in RMS and bibliographic sources; authors and reviewers may not follow the same naming conventions, and homonymous names (namesakes) create ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement fuzzy matching, canonicalization, and disambiguation algorithms; account for variations (initials, ordering, diacritics). Antipattern: naive string-equality checks that miss matches or create false positives due to homonyms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation of bibliographic identifiers and input data
rubrics_metrics.description: Some venues demand explicit bibliographic identifiers (e.g., DBLP ids), but users may enter invalid or incorrect links to DBLP or Google Scholar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate user-supplied identifiers and links; build checks for plausibility and cross-reference with other sources. Treat user-provided identifiers as helpful hints but not authoritative without validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple bibliographic and data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: To mitigate single-source errors and missing data, COI detection should leverage multiple data sources (e.g., DBLP plus RMS records and other bibliographies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate and reconcile data from multiple sources to improve recall and precision. Guidance: avoid over-dependence on one source because DBLP or others can have misattributions or missing entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explainability and justification for flagged COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tools must generate explanations to justify why a specific author-reviewer pair is marked as COI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide human-readable evidence (e.g., co-authored papers, shared affiliations, dates) so PC chairs can assess and act; make explanations prominent in reports. Antipattern: black-box flags with no supporting evidence that PC chairs cannot verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph-based visualization of relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide graph-views of co-authorship relationships between authors, reviewers, and meta-reviewers for each conflict paper to make results accessible to PC chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visualizations to summarize connection paths (direct coauthor, two-hop links, shared institution) and help chairs reason about whether a tie constitutes a policy violation or a borderline case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-based violation detection and configurable thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The system should generate reports on 'possible COI violations based on a venue's COI policy' (e.g., co-authorship within last x years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the policy parameters configurable (x, y, what counts as 'worked together closely') so venues can enforce their own rules. Also expose which policy rule triggered a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic integration and RMS-independence
rubrics_metrics.description: COI detection tooling should be orthogonal to the RMS's 'secret sauce' for reviewer assignment, making it generic and extensible to any RMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design APIs or adapters to ingest reviewer assignments and submission metadata from multiple RMS platforms. Avoid tight coupling to any single RMS so the tool can be reused across venues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for journal workflows and AE-reviewer discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal review systems often lack COI management frameworks and even lacking reviewer-AE discussion infrastructure; automated COI tools should extend to journals (e.g., J-CLOSET).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide workflows suitable for journals: AE-level checks during reviewer assignment, facilities for private AE-reviewer discussion about COI, and integration with editorial systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisit and rationalize COI policy thresholds (evidence-based policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common rules (e.g., co-authorship-based COI limited to last x years) are ad hoc and lack scientific basis; COI may persist beyond arbitrary year cutoffs and should be consistent across venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage communities to re-evaluate thresholds and pursue evidence-based or uniform policies. Provide analytics to study historical co-authorship patterns to inform policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect submarine COI (indirect/contextual ties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submarine COI: bias between two people that is not captured by explicit ties like co-authorship or same institution (contextual/dynamic relationships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research and develop methods (possibly leveraging contextual signals or content analysis) to identify less explicit relationships; surface borderline cases for human review. Acknowledge that fully automatic detection is hard and such cases may need human input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect torpedo COI (antagonistic bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Torpedo COI: antagonistic relationships or topic-based antagonism that may lead to unfavorable (or favorable) biased reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complement explicit COI detection with review-content or historical-behavior signals where appropriate; prioritize human adjudication for suspected antagonistic bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic features for oversight (bid analytics, publication profiles, PC diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide additional analytics such as bid analytics to find interesting patterns, publication profiles of PC members, and analysis of PC diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analytics to detect anomalies or systemic patterns (e.g., repeated assignments between close collaborators) and to support fairness/diversity goals. Present findings in actionable reports for chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scalability to PC size and submission volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Manual double-checking of COI is impractical at typical conference scales (PC lists up to ~200 and many submissions); COI management must scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the automated system can process large numbers of submissions and reviewers efficiently and produce prioritized, digestible outputs for chairs rather than unmanageable long lists of flags.
